explanation: No single theme. The strongest cases are function words (' of', ' the') inside boilerplate license text ('Neither the name of', 'See the License', 'reproduce the above'), but equally strong hits land on unrelated tokens: a '{' in LaTeX, a UUID digit, '(\'' in PHP, a sentence-ending period, 'head' in 'headsets', Japanese text. Mid and weak hits are scattered word pieces.

Fires on pieces of abbreviation and citation markup: the '.S'/'.Sc' after B or M in degree names (B.S., M.Sc., Bachelor's), and the 'B'/'ref' token right after '[@' in academic citation keys ('[@B3]', '[@ref6]'). Weaker offshoots are 'BSD-style' in license headers and code tokens like 'namespace' and '.com' in URLs. Ordinary prose words fire only weakly.

Fires in scientific-abstract prose (biomedical or technical, often written in Chinese-English style) on connective or structural tokens: commas after an opening clause ('recently,', 'methods,'), 'aspects', 'according', 'based', 'leads', 'is caused', 'The aim of this study was', 'Thus', 'Therefore'. Strongest at the discourse junctions of abstract sentences. It is weak in non-academic text.

Fires on the tag-name token right after '<' in HTML/XML markup, strongest for '<a' (anchors in lists or nav) and also 'option', 'li', 'string', 'label', 'span', 'h3'/'h4', plus the attribute name 'value'. Weaker on other attribute or quote tokens inside tags. Plain text gets almost nothing.

Fires on tokens in PHP-ecosystem code and discussions: namespace backslashes and class paths ('\Psr', 'Symfony\Component\', 'Zend/Pdf'), PHP error messages ('Uncaught exception', 'E_STRICT', '... in /home'), '__construct', 'extends', 'use' statements, and mentions of PHP/Magento/Laravel. Other languages give only weak responses.

Fires on a word-initial fragment of a word split into several subword tokens, usually a capitalized or uncommon word in any language or in code ('J[av]itz', 'L[ints]', 'N[al]bari', 'P[open]', 'P[IVOT]', 'up[sert]', 'zurück', Greek and Finnish fragments, 'E.g.'). The common thread is the start of a rare or multi-piece word, not its meaning. A loose, diffuse pattern.

Fires on the token 'form'/'Form' and words built on it (Form, -forming, formaldehyde, Formel, formatters, Formalism, subform, 'se formou'), in any sense: a web form, a shape, 'in form', a chemical name. Strongest when 'form' is a standalone or compound piece, and weaker for 'formation' or related ideas such as 'morph' and 'style'.

Fires on the last piece of a multi-token name or identifier, mostly the trailing digit or letter of an alphanumeric code (p53, B12, F-35, A66, Android 5.1, GLP-1, H-1B, Blender3D), and also word endings that complete a proper name or rare word ('Gilmour', 'Vernon', 'wholegrain', 'multifocal', 'Elmer'). The unit fires as the entity is completed.

Fires mainly on 'settle' and its family (settled, settle in, settle for or on, settlement, settlers, a score to settle). Secondary jobs are 'turn around' (strong) and 'still' (moderate, as in 'are still missing', 'fewer still'). Unrelated pieces are weak.

Fires on mid-word subword fragments, especially the second or third piece of a word in non-English text (Spanish 'dif|undir', Portuguese 'f|izesse', Dutch 'z|it', German 'Milbenk|ä|se', Hungarian, CJK byte pieces), and on split capitalized pieces in English ('Ocasio-C|ortez', 'F|UND', 'C|ANNOT'). A loose tokenization-level pattern with no shared meaning.

Fires on the final subword piece that completes a technical or scientific multi-token term ('sh|iny', 'nplur|als', 'liquid crystal', 'crystal display', 'reverse phase', 'di|odes', 'Ultr|ason|ography', 'Longitud|inal', 'com|edy'). There are also unrelated strong hits on 'I' in first-person opinion statements and on random digits. The term-completion part is the main signal, but the set is mixed.

Fires on a word that continues a formal noun phrase, most often a preposition or noun right after a head word in legal or scientific prose: court names ('Court of Criminal Appeals', 'Superior Court', 'JUDGE'), 'licensed to', 'filed against', 'parents of', 'families with', 'sample of', 'toxic to'. In practice: function words that link a head noun to its complement in formal text.

Fires on approximation adverbs meaning 'nearly': 'almost' (strongest), 'nearly', 'virtually', 'just about', and Spanish 'casi', typically before quantifiers or absolutes ('almost none', 'almost always', 'nearly every'). Other words get only weak, scattered activation.

Fires on the leading indentation whitespace of the first statement line inside a newly opened code block (a function, method, constructor or loop body), right after a line ending in '{' or '=> {'. Weaker on indentation of later lines and on comment or blank-line boundaries.

Fires on the token right after a word that sets up a contrast or qualifier: a version number after a product name ('angular 1.x', 'iOS 6', 'IE 10'), a suffix that completes a technical adjective ('non-digest|ible', 'water-sol|uble', 'Class|ical', 'off|ine'), or the second item of a pair ('wholesale and retail', 'small ... or large'). The examples are diverse and no clear single concept fits.

Fires on ' of' in the patent section heading '2. Description of the (Prior/Related) Art' (very consistent), and on ' by' in 'Written by'. Smaller offshoots are tokens in legal headers (initials, dates). In general it fires on the connective inside a stock document-section or byline formula.

No clear common feature. Strong hits include the end of a name ('Clap|ton', 'NSCL|C', 'melan|omas'), 'copy of' in GPL license text, 'death penalty', 'grant the motion', 'have the meaning', 'public void', '// Do any', and a German opening quotation mark. These look like predictable continuations inside stock phrases, but the domains are unrelated.

Fires on the head noun of a compound noun phrase, where the token is the main noun after a modifier ('K+ current', 'IC chip', 'SMS messages', 'trait test anxiety', 'wound surface', 'mRNA'). Also strong on 'House' (House Speaker, Households, Housewives). There are scattered hits on mid-word fragments. Broadly 'core noun of a domain-specific compound', but noisy.

A mixture of several fixed patterns: 'you' in 'Can you ...?' questions, 'half' in 'second/first half (of)', 'relative' in 'X relative to Y' (patent language), and the final segment of a Java/Swift import or member name ('.OnClickListener', '.viewDidLoad', 'ZonedDateTime'), plus scattered others ('NATO', 'slippery').

Fires on a word that opens a pending specification, where the text is about to say exactly which or what: 'the patient group that', 'the precise/exact/optimal/underlying ...', 'when', 'who', 'how', 'figure out', and 'For the full copyright and license information' in headers. It also fires on config or key-name pieces in code. Mostly about a precise detail that remains unknown or still to be specified.

Fires on function words and connectives inside software license and copyright header boilerplate ('released under the MIT License', 'See License.txt in the project root for license information', 'free of charge,', 'bundled with', 'can be found in the LICENSE file', 'regarding copyright'). Text outside such headers fires only weakly, for example a comment like 'In a real world app,'.
